records.sourceFile: Review of media representation of sport concussion and implications for youth sports.pdf

paper.citation: Jeckell AS, Fontana RS, Gonzalez R. Review of media representation of sport concussion and implications for youth sports. Clin Sports Med 2023.
paper.abstract: This narrative review examined 20 Google News articles on sport-related concussion published 2012-2022, counting terms such as concussion, CTE, retirement and dementia, and summarized research on how athletes, parents and coaches understand and report concussion. The authors conclude that media coverage can misrepresent concussion and that clinicians should correct misconceptions among patients and athletes.
paper.tldr: Media coverage of concussion often uses misleading terms and emphasizes CTE and retirement, which can encourage fear about youth sport. Clinicians should ask where patients get concussion information and correct misunderstandings about risk and recovery.
paper.methods: Narrative review combining a random sample of 20 Google News articles (from 25 selected from the first 100 search results, after excluding those behind subscriptions or cookie walls) published 2012-2022, with counts of key terms per article, and a summary of the literature on concussion epidemiology, youth sport participation, and athlete and parent knowledge.
paper.findings: All 20 articles mentioned concussion, 13 mentioned CTE, 10 mentioned dementia, 9 mentioned retirement, and 'mild' or 'minor' described concussion in 7. The authors cite prior studies reporting that 15% to 45% of collegiate athletes choose not to report suspected concussion, and that accurate knowledge does not reliably lead to reporting. They also report that 96% of parents believed there are long-term effects of concussion, as cited from a prior survey.
paper.limitations: The media sample was a random selection of 20 articles from one search engine's news results rather than a systematic search, and the literature summary is narrative with no quality grading. The authors do not measure how media changes athletes' or parents' behavior. The Discussion reports retirement in 50% of articles, while the Results and Table 1 give 9 of 20 (45%).
paper.practicalImplications: Ask patients and athletes where they get concussion information, and correct common misconceptions about CTE, long-term risk and phrases such as 'ding' or 'bell rung'. Stress full recovery and return to baseline before full return to sport, and note the authors' view that complete removal from all sport is rarely necessary.
paper.athleteDev: Staff should expect athletes and parents to arrive with fears from media coverage, which can affect participation and symptom reporting. Encourage prompt symptom reporting, since the review notes athletes often hide symptoms to avoid losing playing time.
paper.rtp: The review supports a full recovery and return to baseline before full return to sport, but it does not set return-to-play criteria or timelines. Use it to frame education and symptom-reporting expectations, not as a clinical return-to-play protocol.

records.sourceFile: Targeting Rule Implementation Decreases Neck Injuries in High School Football - A National Injury Surveillance Study.pdf

paper.citation: Obana KK, Mueller JD, Zhong JR, et al. Targeting rule implementation decreases neck injuries in high school football: a national injury surveillance study. The Physician and Sportsmedicine 2021.
paper.abstract: This retrospective NEISS analysis of high school football players aged 14-18 compared emergency department neck injuries before (2009-2013) and after (2015-2019) the 2014 NFHS targeting rule. Average yearly overall neck injuries fell from 5,278 to 3,481 and helmet-to-helmet injuries from 851 to 508; injuries with an unspecified mechanism also fell significantly, while the other named mechanisms did not change significantly.
paper.tldr: Emergency department neck injuries among high school football players fell after the 2014 targeting rule, especially helmet-to-helmet injuries. The study cannot prove the rule caused the drop, but it supports continued enforcement of rules against targeting.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of NEISS data for football-related neck injuries (product codes 1211 and 89) in players aged 14-18, January 2009 to December 2019. Narratives were reviewed to exclude non-organized or non-football injuries and to code mechanism, setting, loss of consciousness and injury type. Poisson regression and t-tests compared pre- and post-rule periods, with 2014 removed.
paper.findings: Post-rule years had fewer neck injuries than pre-rule years (average 3,481 vs 5,278 per year, P=0.004), helmet-to-helmet injuries fell (508 vs 851, P=0.04), and unspecified-mechanism injuries fell (2,265 vs 3,546, P=0.002). Neck injuries were already declining across 2009-2019 (Poisson coefficient -0.0121 per year, P=0.0003), and the post-rule period remained significantly lower than the pre-rule reference (coefficient -0.3454, P<0.0001), with a rise again in 2019. Strains made up 59.8% of injuries, and 52.0% of injuries with a known setting occurred in competition vs 48.0% in practice.
paper.limitations: Only emergency department visits are captured, so milder injuries managed by athletic trainers or clinics are missed, and 67% of injuries lacked mechanism detail. The before-and-after design cannot establish causation, and the Discussion's pre-rule average (5,287) differs slightly from the Results (5,278).
paper.practicalImplications: Support enforcement of the targeting rule and limit helmet-to-helmet contact in practice as well as games, since neck injuries with a known setting occurred about equally in both. Treat the rule change as associated with fewer ED-treated neck injuries rather than proven to cause the drop.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure performance or tackling technique. Its use for coaching staff is limited to supporting rules and practice plans that reduce helmet-to-helmet contact, where nearly half of these injuries occurred.
paper.rtp: The study counts emergency department diagnoses and does not address return-to-play decisions after a neck injury, so it cannot guide clearance. Injuries handled only by athletic trainers or clinics are not captured.

records.sourceFile: A systematic review of effects on ACL injury of soccer shoe outsoles, soccer playing field surfaces, and outsole-surface interface.pdf

paper.citation: Cicchella A, He J. A systematic review of effects on ACL injury of soccer shoe outsoles, soccer playing field surfaces, and outsole-surface interface. Encyclopedia 2024;4:888-899.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of 58 papers examines how soccer shoe outsoles, playing surfaces and the outsole-surface interface relate to ACL injury. The authors identify outsole design, shear and rotational forces, artificial turf characteristics, surface aging and weather as the main biomechanical factors.
paper.tldr: Boot stud design and playing surface both change traction, and traction is linked to forces on the knee, but the evidence does not show which combination lowers ACL injury risk. Staff should treat boots and pitch condition as exposures to monitor, not as proven fixes.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus, with reference-list searching and an external expert check. Studies had to address soccer outsoles or playing surfaces and ACL injury mechanics, be peer-reviewed English articles in SCI-indexed journals, and not be narrative reviews. From 252 search results, 84 full texts were assessed and 58 papers were included.
paper.findings: Outsole type made little difference to translational or rotational traction except for soft-ground and turf designs, and soft-ground boots gave the highest rotational traction on natural grass. Artificial turf produced greater rotational traction than natural grass in several experiments, and drier soil and higher air temperatures on natural grass were associated with higher traction. Cited epidemiology is mixed: several studies found similar overall injury rates on artificial and natural turf, one reported 30-50% higher lower-extremity injury rates on artificial turf, and none isolated ACL effects.
paper.limitations: Epidemiological data cannot separate surface effects from weather, grass conditions and playing time, and many experiments are old, laboratory-based or cadaveric. The authors describe AXIS quality appraisal but report no quality results, found no comparative studies of hybrid surfaces, and note there is no universal index of cleat performance for ACL risk. The abstract's statement that ACL injuries 'dramatically increase' on artificial surfaces is not supported by the reviewed epidemiology.
paper.practicalImplications: Consider boot stud type and pitch condition together, since outsole type, surface type, moisture and temperature all change traction. Field condition can drift with wear, and the authors note worn fields may not match FIFA standards, so checking pitch condition across a season is reasonable. The review does not identify any boot or surface that reduces ACL injury.
paper.athleteDev: Track boot type and pitch condition (wear, moisture, temperature) as part of the injury-risk picture, since traction changes with each. The review does not show which combination lowers ACL risk, so use it to flag exposures rather than to prescribe equipment.
paper.rtp: The review concerns ACL injury mechanisms and prevention, not return to play after an ACL injury, so it cannot guide clearance or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Orthopaedic consequences of modern gladiators - A systematic review of lower extremity musculoskeletal issues in retired NFL players.pdf

paper.citation: McClure M, Cooke B, Elphingstone J, et al. Orthopaedic consequences of modern gladiators: a systematic review of lower extremity musculoskeletal issues in retired NFL players. The Physician and Sportsmedicine 2022.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of nine studies with 16,593 retired NFL players examines lower extremity musculoskeletal outcomes after retirement. The authors report arthritis prevalence more than twice that of US males, osteoarthritis in about 37% of players, and higher hip and knee replacement rates than the general population, especially under age 50.
paper.tldr: Retired NFL players have more arthritis and joint replacement than the general population, and these rates rise with repeated lower-extremity injuries. The evidence is mostly survey-based, so the size of the risk is approximate.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of CENTRAL, Scopus, Medline, PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar searched to February 2021. Two reviewers screened studies of retired NFL players with lower extremity injury, osteoarthritis or arthroplasty outcomes, and risk of bias was rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Nine studies were included, and pooled prevalence and chi-square and relative risk comparisons were made against general-population data.
paper.findings: Lower extremity injury prevalence ranged from 44% to 79% across studies, and pooled osteoarthritis prevalence (body-wide, not joint-specific) was about 37%. In one survey, arthritis, defined broadly to include rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia, was 2.2 times as prevalent as in US males (95% CI 2.1-2.3), and players under 50 had 16.1 and 13.8 times higher TKA and THA risk, respectively, per the text. Osteoarthritis prevalence rose with lower-extremity injuries, for example from 26% with none to 44% with two or more in one study.
paper.limitations: The authors note the included studies are level III-IV evidence with some lacking standardized protocols or adequate sample sizes, heterogeneous outcomes, that most osteoarthritis data are body-wide rather than lower-extremity specific, and that statistical pooling was only possible for arthroplasty and limited arthritis data. Only professional football was studied, and the authors suggest including high school, college and other contact sports.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest standardized musculoskeletal evaluation as players leave the league, weight management after retirement, and attention to knee ligament and ankle injury prevention. These recommendations follow from the link between repeated injuries, obesity and later osteoarthritis, but the review did not test any of these interventions directly.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes with a long career ahead, the review suggests joint health is affected by repeated lower-extremity injuries, so reconditioning and injury prevention matter for life after sport. It does not give training prescriptions or performance measures.
paper.rtp: The review covers long-term musculoskeletal outcomes after retirement, not return to play after an injury, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. It supports longer-term follow-up of joint health after athletes leave the sport.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring musculotendon mechanics of prospectively injured elite rugby athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Kenneally-Dabrowski C, Brown NAT, Serpell BG, Perriman D, Spratford W, Sutherland A, et al. Hamstring musculotendon mechanics of prospectively injured elite rugby athletes. Research in Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: Two elite rugby union players had hamstring musculotendon mechanics estimated during pre-season high-speed running, before each later sustained a hamstring injury in competition. Measurements used motion capture, force plates, hamstring MRI and musculoskeletal modelling. The biceps femoris long head had the greatest strain of the hamstring muscles during late swing, and its force relative to muscle capacity was highest in one athlete and similar to semimembranosus in the other.
paper.tldr: In two elite rugby players who later injured a hamstring, the biceps femoris long head showed the highest modelled strain during late swing sprinting. This is a hypothesis-generating case series, not proof of an injury mechanism.
paper.methods: Two elite male rugby union players completed three maximal 50 m sprints during pre-season on a 20-camera motion capture system with force plates, and hamstring MRI was taken within 48 hours. Muscle volumes gave physiological cross-sectional area, and an OpenSim model with computed muscle control estimated musculotendon strain, force and power during late swing.
paper.findings: Peak strain was greatest in the biceps femoris long head in both athletes (7.07% and 9.31%). Peak force relative to body mass was greatest in semimembranosus. Relative to muscle capacity, biceps femoris long head force was highest in Athlete A (120.8 N/PCSA) and similar to semimembranosus in Athlete B. Injuries occurred 139 and 192 days after testing, and Athlete A's injury was in the right biceps femoris long head.
paper.limitations: Two athletes only, with no control group, and the model used generic rather than subject-specific muscle inputs. Athlete A had three prior left hamstring injuries, and Athlete B's injury was not assessed by MRI. The abstract says biceps femoris long head had the greatest force relative to capacity, but Table 1 shows semimembranosus slightly higher in Athlete B (110.89 vs 109.38 N/PCSA).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can treat high late-swing biceps femoris long head load and strain as a plausible hypothesis to test in larger samples. The paper does not support using this modelling to screen individual athletes, since it requires MRI and laboratory equipment and was not tested as a predictor of injury.
paper.athleteDev: The findings describe how hamstring loads may be distributed during fast running in two athletes. They do not show that any sprint training change reduces hamstring injury risk, so they should not be used to set training targets.
paper.rtp: This study cannot guide return to sport decisions. It reports pre-injury measurements in two athletes and does not test rehabilitation, running load progression or readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Calf muscle injury in elite athletics - An 8-season prospective cohort study.pdf

paper.citation: Kelly S, Polglass G, Giakoumis M, Pollock N, Shaw JW. Calf muscle injury in elite athletics: an 8-season prospective cohort study. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2025.
paper.abstract: Indirect calf muscle injury was recorded prospectively over eight seasons in 201 elite track and field athletes (616 athlete-seasons). There were 85 injuries, a third of them severe, with the soleus most often affected. The raw incidence was 0.14 medical-attention injuries per athlete-season, and older age and previous lower-limb injury were associated with higher incidence, while sex was not.
paper.tldr: About one in nine elite track and field athletes had a calf muscle injury each season, and soleus injuries carried the largest time-loss burden and recurrence. Older athletes and those with previous lower-limb injury had higher rates, though these are associations from an observational study.
paper.methods: Prospective observational study of British Athletics World Class Programme athletes from December 2011 to November 2019, with injuries diagnosed clinically and recorded in an athlete management system. Injuries were classified by time loss, severity, muscle and onset. Poisson regression models examined age, sex and event group, and the results also report the count of previous lower-limb injuries.
paper.findings: There were 85 calf injuries, 77 of them time-loss, and 52 involved the soleus (61%). The incidence was 0.14 medical-attention injuries per athlete-season (95% CI 0.11 to 0.17), with male and female rates not significantly different. Each additional year of age was associated with 1.09 times the medical-attention incidence (p = .0025) and 1.11 times the time-loss incidence (p = .005). Each previous lower-limb injury was associated with 1.21 times the medical-attention incidence (p = .025), but not time-loss incidence. Mean time loss was 29 days, 33% of injuries were severe, and 14 injuries were recurrences.
paper.limitations: Exposure was measured per athlete-season, not per hour, and injuries were not graded with BAMIC or re-examined by imaging for all cases. Power was low for sex (about 18%), and the previous-injury effect was not significant for time-loss, although the abstract describes a significant effect for previous lower-limb injury without this distinction. Only 85 injuries were recorded, which limits between-event comparisons.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff working with elite track and field athletes can expect calf injury to be common, with soleus injuries the most frequent and most disruptive. Injury counts peaked in April, ahead of the summer season, and the authors suggest increasing prevention efforts before that period, although no prevention strategy was tested. Older athletes and those with previous lower-limb injury may merit closer attention, but the study does not show that monitoring reduces injury.
paper.athleteDev: Calf injuries in this cohort were often severe, with a mean time loss of 29 days, and counts peaked in April before the summer competition season. The study describes injury patterns by event group, not the effect of any training change, so it does not show which programme changes would lower calf injury risk.
paper.rtp: The study can inform expected severity and recurrence, with recurrences occurring a mean of 364 days after the index injury and a median of 214 days. It does not test rehabilitation or return-to-training criteria, so these timings should not be used as a fixed return-to-sport timeline.

records.sourceFile: Sprint running mechanics are associated with hamstring strain injury - A 6-month prospective cohort study of 126 elite male footballers.pdf

paper.citation: Bramah C, Rhodes S, Clarke-Cornwell A, Dos'Santos T. Sprint running mechanics are associated with hamstring strain injury: a 6-month prospective cohort study of 126 elite male footballers. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort study scored sprint running mechanics in 126 professional male footballers with the Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score (S-MAS), a video-based screen, and followed them for six months. Higher S-MAS scores were found in players with previous sprint-related hamstring injury and in players who later sustained one. After adjusting for age and previous injury, each one-point increase in S-MAS was associated with a 33% higher rate of new sprint-related hamstring injury.
paper.tldr: Players with poorer sprint mechanics on a video-based screen had a higher rate of later sprint-related hamstring injury. The screen is quick to use, but its accuracy for predicting injury is modest, so it should be one part of a wider screening process.
paper.methods: Players from eight English Football League clubs were filmed during two maximal 35 m sprints at 240 fps, in pre-season or in-season. A single blinded biomechanist scored each sprint with the 12-item S-MAS. Clubs reported new hamstring injuries monthly for six months, confirmed by MRI. Poisson regression estimated incidence rate ratios, adjusted for age and previous hamstring injury, and ROC analysis chose the cut-off.
paper.findings: In the retrospective analysis of 118 players, those with a previous sprint-related hamstring injury had higher S-MAS scores (median 6 vs 5, p = 0.007). In the prospective analysis of 92 players, 14 had a sprint-related injury, with median S-MAS 6 vs 4 (p = 0.006). The unadjusted IRR was 1.38 per point (95% CI 1.06 to 1.79), and the adjusted IRR was 1.33 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.76, p = 0.044). A cut-off of 5.5 gave sensitivity 78.6%, specificity 65.4% and AUC 0.732. The categorical IRR was 2.8 (95% CI 0.94 to 8.35, p = 0.065), which was not significant.
paper.limitations: The S-MAS was not validated against 3D motion capture and was scored by one experienced rater. Training and match load were not monitored, and players with other severe non-hamstring time loss were removed from the uninjured group. The power calculation used the same data as the analysis, and seven players were lost to follow-up. Only male players were studied, and players were followed for different parts of the season.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners can use the S-MAS from routine sprint video to flag players whose sprint mechanics may be suboptimal, particularly those with a previous hamstring injury. Because sensitivity and specificity are modest, a flagged score should prompt a wider review of strength, load and injury history rather than a decision on its own.
paper.athleteDev: The S-MAS is a video-based sprint technique screen that could be used alongside performance testing to track running mechanics across a season. The study does not show that changing sprint technique reduces hamstring injury, so it should not be used as a stand-alone target for training changes.
paper.rtp: The study does not test return to sport. It suggests that sprint mechanics may be neglected in rehabilitation after a previous sprint-related hamstring injury, but it does not show that retraining mechanics restores readiness or lowers reinjury risk.

records.sourceFile: Early vs delayed lengthening exercises for acute hamstring injury in male athletes - A randomized controlled clinical trial.pdf

paper.citation: Vermeulen R, Whiteley R, van der Made AD, van Dyk N, Almusa E, Geertsema C, et al. Early versus delayed lengthening exercises for acute hamstring injury in male athletes: a randomised controlled clinical trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: Ninety male athletes with an MRI-confirmed acute hamstring injury were randomised to add lengthening (eccentric) exercises either on day 1 of a standard rehabilitation programme or after they could run at 70% of maximal speed. Time to return to sport did not differ between the groups (adjusted HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.60), and neither did reinjury rates over 12 months. Early introduction did not shorten return to sport or lower reinjury risk, though the median difference of 8 days favoured the early group.
paper.tldr: Starting lengthening exercises on day 1 rather than after about 70% running speed did not change return-to-sport time or reinjury rates in male athletes with acute hamstring injuries. The median return was about 8 days sooner in the early group, but this was not statistically significant.
paper.methods: Single-centre, parallel-group, randomised superiority trial at the Aspetar sports medicine hospital in Qatar, with blinded assessors and a blinded statistician. Both groups followed the same six-stage criteria-based programme, differing only in when Askling lengthening exercises began. Primary outcome was days to full training or match play, analysed by Cox regression (intention to treat). Reinjury was followed by telephone at 2, 6 and 12 months.
paper.findings: Median return to sport was 23 days (IQR 16 to 35) in the early group and 33 days (IQR 23 to 40) in the delayed group. The unadjusted HR was 1.15 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.84, p=0.57), and the adjusted HR was 0.95 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.60, p=0.84). Reinjury within 2 months was 8.8% early and 8.3% delayed, with no significant differences at 2 to 6 or 6 to 12 months. Eccentric strength at 60 degrees per second was higher in the early group at return to sport (198 Nm vs 182 Nm, p=0.029), but no other outcome differed.
paper.limitations: Loss to follow-up was 19% against a planned 10%, handled by a consensus-based return-to-sport date that was not in the protocol, and reinjury data were missing for 20% to 28% of participants. The trial was sized for a 6.6-day difference and the authors note it is potentially underpowered, and treating clinicians could not be blinded to group. The Results text gives the 2-month reinjury percentages in reverse compared with Table 3 (Table 3: early 8.8%, delayed 8.3%).
paper.practicalImplications: Starting lengthening exercises on day 1 of rehabilitation after a grade I or II hamstring strain in men produced similar reinjury rates to a delayed start, but reinjuries were few and the confidence intervals were wide (2-month OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.18 to 5.0). The trial did not show a significant reduction in time to return, although the 8-day median difference and possible underpowering mean a benefit cannot be ruled out, so timing can rest on the individual clinical picture.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff may note that the early group had higher eccentric knee flexor strength at return to sport, but this was a secondary outcome in a small trial and was not the focus of the study. It does not show that early lengthening improves sprint or running performance.
paper.rtp: This trial directly informs return-to-sport planning for male athletes with MRI-confirmed grade I or II acute hamstring injury. Starting lengthening exercises early did not significantly change time to return or reinjury rate, so it should not be used to predict a specific return date. It does not apply to women, grade III injuries or injuries without MRI confirmation.

records.sourceFile: What is the evidence for and   validity of return to sport testing after ACL reconstruction surgery - A   systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Webster KE, Hewett TE. What is the evidence for and validity of return-to-sport testing after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction surgery? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2019;49:917-929.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) return-to-sport (RTS) test batteries. Across 18 studies, only 23% of patients passed the batteries before returning to sport. Passing was linked to lower graft rupture risk and higher contralateral ACL injury risk, while the overall ACL re-injury risk was not significantly different. The authors conclude the evidence on the validity of current batteries is equivocal.
paper.tldr: Only about one in four patients pass ACL return-to-sport test batteries, and passing was not associated with a clear reduction in overall ACL re-injury risk. Passing was associated with lower graft rupture risk but higher contralateral ACL injury risk, so the batteries cannot yet be relied on as a safety clearance.
paper.methods: Five databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and SPORTDiscus) were searched to May 2018, following PRISMA. Studies of ACLR patients that reported how many passed a full RTS battery were included. Pooled pass rates used random-effects proportion meta-analysis, and subsequent injury was analysed with risk ratio meta-analysis. Overlapping patient groups were excluded from the same pooled analysis.
paper.findings: Before return to sport, 23% of patients passed RTS batteries (95% CI 8% to 43%, I2 97.5%, eight studies, 876 patients). After return to strenuous sport, the pass rate was also 23% (95% CI 18% to 29%, three studies). For any knee injury, RR was 0.28 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.94, p = 0.09, two studies). For any ACL injury, RR was 0.80 (95% CI 0.27 to 2.3, p = 0.7, five studies). Graft rupture RR was 0.40 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.69, p < 0.001), and contralateral ACL injury RR was 3.35 (95% CI 1.52 to 7.37, p = 0.003). One study found that patients who passed at 6 months were more likely to have returned to sport at 12 months (81% vs 44%).
paper.limitations: Only one included study assessed return to sport and only five reported subsequent injury, with small samples and broad inclusion criteria (age limits typically 14 to 50 years, mixed graft types and sports) and no control of confounders or exposure. RTS definitions and follow-up varied, and overlapping patient groups were handled by excluding some studies from the same pooled analysis. For any knee injury the Results report RR 0.28 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.94, p = 0.09), but the Discussion describes the interval as a 93% reduction to a 21% increase, so the printed CI is inconsistent with the non-significant result.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not present a passed test battery as proof that ACL re-injury risk has fallen, because the pooled evidence does not show a reduction in overall ACL injury. Because only 23% of patients pass batteries, most reconstructed athletes will fail some criteria, and staff should decide on return using the wider clinical picture. Monitoring both knees is advisable, given the signal of higher contralateral ACL injury among those who passed.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff may use test results to track rehabilitation progress, but a pass on a battery does not confirm that an athlete is ready for high performance demands. The one study that linked passing to later return to sport is a single observational report, so it should not be used to set performance targets.
paper.rtp: This review is directly relevant to return-to-sport decisions after ACL reconstruction, but it shows that test batteries have uncertain validity for deciding safe return. Passing a battery was not associated with a lower overall ACL injury risk and was associated with a higher contralateral injury risk, so it should not by itself clear an athlete to return. The review does not define a validated pass rule or cut-off, so it cannot say which battery or threshold makes return safe.
